newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea shrugs off Pyongyang threat on peace talks.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea shrugs off Pyongyang threat on peace talks.

text.p: South Korea on Tuesday shrugged off a threat by rival North Korea to spurn peace talks proposed by Seoul and Washington, saying it was part of Pyongyang's routine game of bluff.
The threat highlighted a new obstacle in the already difficult task of trying to lure North Korea into talks to end an armed truce with the South dating from the 1950-53 Korean war.

South Korea insists that peace negotiations cannot take place until Pyongyang apologises over a submarine incursion, and it has withdrawn past offers to brief North Korea on the talks along with the United States.
U.S. officials have indicated they support that position, although an apology from Pyongyang to its arch-foe is almost unthinkable, diplomats say.

On Monday the North Korean foreign ministry accused Washington of backing away from four-way peace talks, including China, proposed by U.S. President Bill Clinton and South Korean head of state Kim Young-sam in April.

"The United States' refusal to make a 'joint explanation' means there is some change in its position," a ministry spokesman was quoted by the official Korean Central News Agency as saying, referring to the proposed briefing.
North Korea was "compelled to interpret this as a revocation of the 'four-way talks'."

"As the United States wants to withdraw its proposal, we have no need to hear any explanation about it," the spokesman said. "We have not had much interest in the proposed 'four-way talks', the content and purpose of which are obscure, still less pinned any hope on them," he added.
South Korea's foreign ministry spokesman dismissed the remarks.
"North Korea is making a tactical move to put pressure on the U.S.. It's a usual move on the part of North Korea in this kind of situation," Suh Dae-won said.

North Korea has used threats and bullying tactics in the past to draw the United States into negotiations. It calculates that Washington, with wider strategic interests in Asia, has more incentive than Seoul to keep inter-Korean dialogue alive.
Nuclear threats by North Korea resulted in a historic agreement with the United States in 1993 for free nuclear reactors that do not produce bomb-grade material.
Pyongyang has not responded officially to the offer of talks intended to establish a permanent peace arrangement in place of the truce.

The submarine dropped off 26 North Koreans on a Southern beach in September, and Seoul says the provocation was a prelude to wider military action. Twenty three of the intruders have been shot dead, one was captured and one is still missing.
"The Korean people believe it is meaningless to start any process now," said Suh, referring to the peace talks. "North Korea must take steps to remedy the situation".

In Japan, which feels threatened by North Korean sabre-rattling, foreign minister Yukihiko Ikeda on Tuesday urged Pyongyang to accept the four-way talks, according to a report by the Kyodo news agency.

"We don't think that the United States has taken back the proposal," Kyodo quoted him telling a news conference. "We hope progress will be made in various ways towards the realisation of the four-way talks."
